item.subject: science
item.chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
item.stem:
Mehak's school fixes its annual day to one month on a purely lunar calendar. Each lunar month begins with a new Moon. Twelve lunar months make about 354 days, while seasons on Earth repeat in about 365 days. After several years the same annual day falls in a different season than it did at first.

Why does a purely lunar calendar not keep the same months aligned with the same seasons year after year?

options.A: Twelve lunar months total about 354 days, which is shorter than the roughly 365-day seasonal year, so the lunar months drift through the seasons.
options.B: A purely lunar calendar stays locked to the seasons because Moon phases and seasons take equal times.
options.C: The seasons themselves become a little longer each year, so the lunar months can no longer keep pace with them.
options.D: Any school calendar that names months, even one not based on Moon phases, must drift from the seasons the same way.
